title: Deployment surface and failure-domain mapping for Hosted / Dedicated / Private
body:
Purpose:
Quick, working reference for how the request surface, failure domains, and tenant fences differ across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. Intended as input to the rollout/upgrade playbooks and the routing policy PRs (esp. region failover + control-plane responsibilities).

Context / motivation:
- We keep getting complex edge cases when a region/instance goes degraded and the fallback behavior depends on deployment mode.
- Need a single, concise mapping engineers can use when designing new routing features (affinity, cost-tier routing, model fallback).
- This is intentionally gritty — contains open questions and TODOs.

High level goals:
- Define where isolation guarantees come from (network, compute, control-plane policy) per mode.
- Clarify which plane (control vs data) owns reroute/fallback decisions.
- Surface operational implications (SLO, metering, egress, upgrades).

Glossary / shorthand used here:
- surface mesh: logical set of ingress points + edge proxies that accept customer requests.
- control-plane shadowing: lightweight control-plane copies deployed in customer region for faster decisions (mostly for Private).
- L0-L3 tenant fence: quick shorthand for levels of tenant isolation we reference below (L0 shared, L1 logical, L2 network, L3 physical).

Summary map (one-line):
- Hosted: shared surface mesh, control-plane decisions centrally, logical fences (L0/L1) + software guardrails, global multi-region failover by policy.
- Dedicated: reserved compute pool per customer (L2/L3), control-plane still coordinates but trust boundary shifts (we avoid touching data plane), routing favors customer-only pools and region affinity.
- Private: control-plane optional (customer-managed); data plane fully customer-controlled (L3). Routing decisions either in-customer or via an API bridge; multi-region patterns are bespoke.

Detailed notes per mode:
1) Hosted (typical SaaS API users)
  - Surface: public API endpoints terminating at our global edge (CDN+edge LB). Requests mapped into multi-tenant fronting proxies that tag tenant id early.
  - Isolation boundary: primarily logical (L0/L1). Tenants isolated by request metadata, RBAC, per-tenant quotas and runtime sandboxes but share kernels + GPUs.
  - Routing responsibilities: central control-plane owns which model variant to route to, cost-tiering, and region preference. The data-plane allows policy-driven fallbacks (eg. degrade to smaller model in same region).
  - Failure domains + failover behavior: when a region degrades we prefer cross-region failover to another hosted region; tenants can opt-out via org policy. We rely on global cache warmers to reduce cold-start latency on failover.
  - Operational considerations: strong telemetry at token-level, enforced rate limits at edge, and transparent per-tenant cost attribution is required for debugging cross-traffic effects.
  - Known tradeoffs: noisy neighbors risk; easier to implement cross-tenant fallback but customers expect predictable latency/cost.

2) Dedicated (reserved capacity / customer GPU pools)
  - Surface: requests land on tenant-dedicated fronting nodes (dedicated pool ingress) or pass through a shared control plane that then pins them to reserved hosts.
  - Isolation boundary: network + compute isolation (L2/L3). VMs/containers/GPU partitions reserved to tenant; we enforce stricter egress and network policies.
  - Routing responsibilities: control-plane manages placement/orchestration but is intentionally conservative about changing the data-path. Failover should prefer other reserved capacity (same tenant) before bursting to hosted pools (if burst allowed by contract).
  - Failure domains + failover behavior: prefer intra-tenant spillover (other racks/availability zones in the same region) -> other regions with dedicated capacity -> last resort: hosted fallback (requires customer opt-in and billing change).
  - Operational considerations: capacity planning and autoscaling decisions are tenant-scoped. Upgrades must preserve tenant pinned versions; canarying is per-tenant and often manual.
  - Known tradeoffs: stronger isolation reduces risk but increases cost and complexity for global failover. Billing/commit tracking needs to be clear when cross-using hosted fallback.

3) Private (VPC / on-prem)
  - Surface: entirely customer-controlled ingress (their LB -> our runtime), or a hybrid where our edge terminates and relays into customer's private network via peering/tunnels.
  - Isolation boundary: full customer control (L3). Our control-plane may be external (shadowed) or self-hosted inside customer infra depending on agreement.
  - Routing responsibilities: typically customer-controlled. If we provide a control-plane bridge, it's limited to non-sensitive decisions (version pins, rollout signals); customer policy enforces final routing.
  - Failure domains + failover behavior: custom — many customers disallow cross-region routing or public-hosted fallback. We provide an optional cross-region replication fabric but it requires customer signoff and network configuration.
  - Operational considerations: on-prem networking, KMS integrations, and audit logs are first-class. Observability is via agent + push model; scraping is more complex.
  - Known tradeoffs: predictable privacy and low surface area we control, but we lose flexibility for automated global failover and cold-start mitigation.

Control-plane vs data-plane split (practical rules):
- Control-plane should make intent-level decisions (preferred region, allowed fallback classes, rollout flags).
- Data-plane must enforce per-request routing, affinity, and fast-fail behavior without synchronous dependence on control-plane for each request.
- For Hosted: control-plane can be authoritative and push policy to edge proxies. For Dedicated: control-plane is authoritative for placement but must avoid unilateral data-path changes. For Private: control-plane is advisory unless explicitly deployed inside customer boundary.

Caching and KV considerations across modes:
- Hosted: cross-tenant cache warming is possible (prefix caching helpful), but must be careful about data leakage. Use tenant-prefixed caches + policy to drop shared entries on tear-down.
- Dedicated: caches are tenant-scoped; eviction policies aligned to tenant SLAs; consistent hashing helps minimize cross-rack cache misses.
- Private: cache behavior is fully customer-controlled. If we offer a central control-plane cache warmer, it must be opt-in and sanitized.

Multi-region specifics and cold-start mitigation:
- Warmers: a lightweight async warmer process that primes KV + model weights in target region before traffic is routed. Hosted mode can run warmers globally; Dedicated only within tenant pools; Private requires customer opt-in.
- Consistent routing keys + sticky affinity windows (e.g., 30s of session affinity) reduce cross-region context rebuilds.

Telemetry & SLO mapping (what to instrument):
- Per-tenant token latency and tail latency (p50/p95/p99).
- Failover rates (per-mode): how often do we cross-region vs intra-region vs fallback-to-hosted.
- Cache miss rates and cold-start durations by region and tenant.
- Billing delta when dedicated tenants use hosted fallback (measure units and bill-capture).

Operational playbook pointers (quick):
- Region partial outage (Hosted): immediate traffic shift policy -> warmers -> alert customers via status -> increase sampling for p99.
- Region partial outage (Dedicated): try intra-tenant spill to other racks -> if unavailable, consult customer-defined fallback policy (do not auto-burst to hosted unless contract permits).
- Private outage: notify customer and provide tooling (image, runbook) for manual failover/restore.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Q1: How do we encode per-tenant fallback policy as a first-class object? (schema + UI + API). Ticket: JIRA-PLAT-2427.
- Q2: Should control-plane shadowing for Private be a supported product feature or a bespoke service? Cost model required.
- Q3: What is the canonical event/metric for "tenant crossed into hosted fallback" so billing + alerts can tie to the same signal?
- TODO: Add concrete examples of routing config YAML for each mode (draft a small sample for Hosted + Dedicated).
- TODO: Add a simple decision diagram for on-call responders (region down -> check dedicated pool -> consult policies -> run warmers).

References & links in text:
- Slack: #platform-routing, #dedicated-ops
- Related Confluence: DEPLOYMENT SURFACE DIAGRAM (linked above)
- Related PR: infra/pull/887 (placement reconciler changes)

Notes to self / scribbles:
- We should avoid a global boolean "allow-hosted-fallback" — instead have a triageable enum: {never, on-contract, attribute-based}.
- Consider a tenant-scoped routing sandbox where we can simulate region failover and pre-warm caches without affecting production.

If you (reader) are making a change to routing or control-plane behavior, please:
1) add a canonical test in the routing-sim harness that exercises cross-region failover for all three modes;
2) add a short section to the PR summary describing which isolation fences are affected;
3) ping @platform-oncall if the change alters default fallback behavior.

-- end of working doc --
